meta.title: "I did it and it happened" — why your child draws false conclusions about causes | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to tell cause from coincidence and stop drawing conclusions from a single event. Game-based course for children aged 8–12.

hero.headline: "I did it and it happened!" — and your child already believes in accidental patterns?
hero.subheadline: "After" doesn't mean "because of". But the brain loves quick conclusions. And that can lead to decisions with no real basis.

media.alt: A child connecting two events and drawing a false conclusion about the cause

pain.title: "After" doesn't mean "because of". But that's exactly how it feels
pain.body:
"I wore these trainers and we won", "I didn't study and got a bad mark — so that must be why", "I did that and everything went wrong". At school, in sport, in everyday life. The child tries to find an explanation — and finds one, but not always the right one.

This isn't illogical thinking — it's the brain working naturally: it looks for connections between events to make sense of the world. But what happened "after" didn't necessarily happen "because of". A coincidence isn't a cause. Without the skill to check, the child starts believing in accidental patterns.

The result — wrong decisions and fears with no real foundation. Lucky trainers, avoiding certain actions, fear of repeating a "mistake" — all of it grows from an unconfirmed connection.

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 8–12 year olds. At this age, children are most receptive to new thinking patterns and haven't yet formed rigid biases.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
